Jeremiah.line: Jeremiah warns Judah of coming judgment through Babylon, calls for repentance, suffers rejection, and promises a future new covenant.
more: God calls Jeremiah as a young prophet to the nations during Judah's final kings.
He condemns idolatry and false worship, urging Judah to return to the LORD.
His messages provoke persecution, imprisonment, and personal laments to God.
He promises restoration after seventy years and a new covenant written on hearts.
Jerusalem falls to Babylon, and Jeremiah is taken to Egypt with a rebellious remnant.
Oracles against the nations close with Babylon's fall and an account of Jerusalem's destruction.

1.line: God calls Jeremiah, appointed before birth, as a prophet to the nations and confirms his message with two visions.
more: Jeremiah protests that he is too young, but God promises to be with him.
God touches his mouth and puts his words there.
An almond branch shows God watching over his word, and a boiling pot signals disaster from the north.
God makes him a fortified city against Judah's kings, priests, and people.

2.line: God charges Israel with abandoning him, the fountain of living waters, for worthless idols and foreign alliances.
more: God recalls Israel's early devotion in the wilderness.
The people have dug broken cisterns that cannot hold water.
Judah is likened to a wild vine and a restless animal in heat.
Though Judah claims innocence, it will be shamed by Egypt as it was by Assyria.

3.line: God calls faithless Israel and Judah to return, promising shepherds, restoration, and Jerusalem as the LORD's throne.
more: Judah is compared to an unfaithful wife, worse than her sister Israel.
Judah's return has been pretense rather than wholehearted.
God promises to gather a remnant to Zion with shepherds after his own heart.
The chapter ends with a model confession of shame and sin.

4.line: God urges Judah to circumcise their hearts and warns of a destroying invader from the north.
more: True repentance would bring blessing to the nations.
A lion from the north will lay Judah's cities waste.
Jeremiah anguishes as he hears the trumpet of war.
He sees the land made formless and empty, yet God will not make a full end.

5.line: God searches Jerusalem for one just person and finds none, so he announces judgment by a distant nation.
more: Both the poor and the great have refused correction.
The people deny that God will act against them.
A nation from afar will devour harvests and cities, yet not make a full end.
Prophets and priests lie, and the people love to have it so.

6.line: Jeremiah warns Jerusalem to flee as a cruel army from the north besieges the city for its wickedness.
more: The people refuse to walk in the ancient paths.
Prophets and priests cry peace when there is no peace.
God rejects their sacrifices because they reject his law.
Jeremiah is made a tester of the people, who prove to be rejected silver.

7.line: At the temple gate Jeremiah warns that trusting in the temple cannot save people who persist in sin.
more: God will do to the temple what he did to Shiloh.
Jeremiah is told not to pray for people who worship the queen of heaven.
God had commanded obedience more than sacrifices.
Child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom will make it the Valley of Slaughter.

8.line: Jeremiah grieves as Judah persists in rebellion, rejects God's law, and faces devastation.
more: Even the bones of kings and priests will be exposed.
Birds know their seasons, but God's people do not know his rules.
The harvest is past, and the people are not saved.
Jeremiah asks whether there is no balm in Gilead.

9.line: Jeremiah weeps over his people's deceit, and God announces exile and mourning for Judah.
more: Neighbors deceive one another and refuse to know the LORD.
Mourning women are summoned to wail over the dead.
Boasting belongs not in wisdom, might, or riches but in knowing the LORD.
God will punish both circumcised Judah and the uncircumcised nations.

10.line: God contrasts lifeless, man-made idols with himself, the living and eternal King and Creator.
more: Idols are decorated wood that cannot speak or walk.
The LORD made the earth by his power and wisdom.
Exile is announced, and Jeremiah mourns his ruined tent.
He asks God to correct him justly and pour out wrath on the nations.

11.line: Judah has broken God's covenant, so disaster is coming, and Jeremiah learns his own townsmen plot to kill him.
more: God reminds Judah of the covenant made at the exodus.
Judah has returned to the sins of its forefathers.
Jeremiah is told not to pray for the people.
Men of Anathoth seek his life, and God promises to punish them.

12.line: Jeremiah asks why the wicked prosper, and God answers that harder trials lie ahead and judgment is coming.
more: God warns that even Jeremiah's family has betrayed him.
God has given his beloved people into the hands of enemies.
Many shepherds have ruined God's vineyard.
Neighboring nations will be uprooted but may be restored if they learn God's ways.

13.line: Jeremiah's ruined linen loincloth pictures how God will spoil Judah's pride, and exile is announced.
more: Jeremiah hides the loincloth by the Euphrates and later finds it useless.
Filled wine jars picture the people filled with drunkenness and destruction.
The king and queen mother are told to humble themselves.
Judah cannot change, as a leopard cannot change its spots.

14.line: During a drought Jeremiah intercedes for Judah, but God refuses their prayers and condemns false prophets.
more: Nobles, farmers, and animals suffer for lack of water.
God says sword, famine, and pestilence will consume the people.
False prophets promising peace will themselves perish.
Jeremiah pleads again, confessing sin and appealing to God's covenant.

15.line: God says even Moses and Samuel could not turn him from judging Judah, and Jeremiah laments his calling.
more: Four kinds of destroyers are appointed because of Manasseh's sins.
Jeremiah regrets his birth and complains of persecution.
He found joy in God's words but feels abandoned.
God calls him to return and promises to make him a bronze wall.

16.line: God forbids Jeremiah to marry, mourn, or feast as signs of coming judgment, yet promises a future return.
more: Sons and daughters in the land will die unmourned.
The sounds of joy and weddings will cease.
A new exodus from the north will surpass the one from Egypt.
The nations will come to admit that idols are worthless.

17.line: Judah's sin is engraved on their hearts, and Jeremiah contrasts trust in man with trust in God.
more: The one who trusts in man is cursed, but trust in the LORD brings blessing.
The heart is deceitful, but God searches it.
Jeremiah prays for healing and vindication against his persecutors.
Keeping the Sabbath would bring blessing, while breaking it would bring fire on Jerusalem.

18.line: At the potter's house God shows he can reshape or destroy a nation, and Judah's leaders plot against Jeremiah.
more: The potter remakes a spoiled vessel as he sees fit.
Judah stubbornly follows its own plans and forgets God.
Enemies plot to silence Jeremiah's words.
Jeremiah asks God to deal with those who seek his harm.

19.line: Jeremiah smashes a clay flask in the Valley of Hinnom to show that God will shatter Jerusalem.
more: Elders and senior priests witness the sign-act.
Judah's idolatry and child sacrifice have filled the place with innocent blood.
The siege will be so severe that people eat their own children.
Jeremiah repeats the warning in the temple court.

20.line: The priest Pashhur beats and imprisons Jeremiah, who then pours out a lament over his calling.
more: Released, Jeremiah renames Pashhur Terror on Every Side and predicts his exile to Babylon.
God's word is like a fire in his bones that he cannot hold in.
He praises God for delivering the needy.
He then curses the day of his birth.

21.line: When King Zedekiah asks for help against Babylon, Jeremiah announces that God himself will fight against Jerusalem.
more: Zedekiah sends Pashhur son of Malchiah to inquire of the LORD.
Pestilence and sword will strike the city, and Zedekiah will be handed to Nebuchadnezzar.
The people are offered life if they surrender to the Chaldeans.
The royal house is called to execute justice.

22.line: Jeremiah warns Judah's kings to do justice and pronounces judgment on Shallum, Jehoiakim, and Coniah.
more: The palace will become a desolation if justice is ignored.
Shallum will die in exile and never return.
Jehoiakim built his house by injustice and will receive a donkey's burial.
Coniah will be cast out, and none of his offspring will sit on David's throne.

23.line: God condemns Judah's failed shepherds and false prophets and promises a righteous Branch from David.
more: God will gather his flock and raise up faithful shepherds.
The coming king will be called The LORD Is Our Righteousness.
False prophets speak dreams from their own minds, not God's word.
Those who misuse the phrase burden of the LORD will be rejected.

24.line: Two baskets of figs show that exiles in Babylon will be restored while Zedekiah and those remaining will be ruined.
more: The vision comes after Jeconiah is taken to Babylon.
God will give the good figs a heart to know him.
The bad figs include those left in Jerusalem and those in Egypt.
They will meet sword, famine, and pestilence.

25.line: Jeremiah announces seventy years of service to Babylon and the cup of God's wrath for all nations.
more: For twenty-three years Judah has ignored his warnings.
After seventy years Babylon itself will be punished.
Jeremiah is told to make many nations drink from the cup.
The LORD roars against all flesh, and the shepherds wail.

26.line: After Jeremiah's temple warning, priests and prophets demand his death, but officials and elders spare him.
more: He repeats that the temple could become like Shiloh.
Elders cite Micah, whom Hezekiah heeded rather than killed.
By contrast, Jehoiakim had the prophet Uriah executed.
Ahikam son of Shaphan protects Jeremiah.

27.line: Wearing a yoke, Jeremiah tells Judah and neighboring kings to submit to Nebuchadnezzar and reject false prophets.
more: God has given these lands to Nebuchadnezzar for a set time.
Nations that serve Babylon will remain in their land.
Zedekiah is urged to submit and live.
The remaining temple vessels will also go to Babylon until God restores them.

28.line: The prophet Hananiah breaks Jeremiah's yoke and predicts quick deliverance, but Jeremiah announces an iron yoke and Hananiah's death.
more: Hananiah says the exiles and vessels will return within two years.
Jeremiah says only fulfillment proves a prophet of peace true.
God replaces the wooden yoke with one of iron.
Hananiah dies that same year.

29.line: Jeremiah writes to the exiles in Babylon to settle down, seek the city's welfare, and await restoration after seventy years.
more: They are to build houses, marry, and pray for Babylon.
God has plans for their welfare, a future and a hope.
The false prophets Ahab and Zedekiah among the exiles are condemned.
Shemaiah, who opposed Jeremiah's letter, is told he will have no descendants.

30.line: God tells Jeremiah to write a book promising that Israel and Judah will be restored after a time of distress.
more: The coming day is called a time of distress for Jacob.
God will break their yoke, and they will serve David their king.
Their wound seems incurable, but God will heal it.
God's wrath will accomplish his purposes in the latter days.

31.line: God promises everlasting love, joyful return, and a new covenant with his law written on his people's hearts.
more: Rachel weeps for her children, but God says they will return.
Ephraim repents, and God has mercy on him.
Each will die for his own sin, not his father's.
Israel's future is as sure as the fixed order of creation.

32.line: During Babylon's siege, imprisoned Jeremiah buys his cousin's field as a sign that land will again be bought in Judah.
more: Zedekiah confines Jeremiah for prophesying the city's fall.
The deeds are sealed and stored in a clay jar.
Jeremiah prays, wondering at God's command amid the siege.
God promises an everlasting covenant and a heart to fear him.

33.line: Still confined, Jeremiah hears God promise to heal Jerusalem and keep his covenant with David and the Levites.
more: God invites Jeremiah to call to him and hear hidden things.
Joy and thanksgiving will return to the ruined places.
A righteous Branch from David will execute justice.
God's covenants are as sure as day and night.

34.line: Jeremiah warns Zedekiah of capture, and Judah is condemned for freeing and then re-enslaving their Hebrew servants.
more: Zedekiah will face Nebuchadnezzar but die in peace.
The people made a covenant to free slaves, then reversed it.
God proclaims to them a liberty to sword, pestilence, and famine.
Babylon's army, now withdrawn, will return and burn the city.

35.line: Jeremiah offers wine to the Rechabites, whose refusal displays a faithfulness that condemns Judah's disobedience.
more: They keep their ancestor Jonadab's commands against wine and houses.
Judah has ignored God's repeated warnings.
Disaster is announced on Judah and Jerusalem.
The Rechabites are promised a descendant always standing before God.

36.line: King Jehoiakim burns the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies, and God has Jeremiah dictate it again.
more: Baruch writes the scroll and reads it in the temple.
Officials hear it and urge Baruch and Jeremiah to hide.
The king cuts the scroll and burns it column by column.
Jehoiakim is told he will have no heir on David's throne.

37.line: Jeremiah warns Zedekiah that Babylon will return, is arrested as a deserter, and is held in the court of the guard.
more: Egypt's army causes Babylon to withdraw for a time.
Jeremiah is beaten and imprisoned in a dungeon cell.
Zedekiah secretly asks for a word, and Jeremiah says he will be handed over.
The king moves him to the court of the guard with daily bread.

38.line: Officials throw Jeremiah into a muddy cistern, Ebed-melech rescues him, and Jeremiah urges Zedekiah to surrender.
more: The officials claim his words weaken the soldiers.
Ebed-melech the Ethiopian gains the king's permission and draws him out.
Jeremiah says surrender will spare Zedekiah and the city.
Zedekiah fears the Judeans and keeps the conversation secret.

39.line: Babylon captures Jerusalem, Zedekiah is blinded and exiled, and Jeremiah and Ebed-melech are spared.
more: Zedekiah flees but is caught near Jericho, and his sons are killed before him.
The city is burned, its walls broken, and many people exiled.
Nebuchadnezzar orders that Jeremiah be treated well.
God promises Ebed-melech his life because he trusted in God.

40.line: Jeremiah chooses to stay in Judah with Governor Gedaliah, who dismisses a warning about an assassination plot.
more: Nebuzaradan releases Jeremiah at Ramah.
Gedaliah urges the remnant to serve Babylon.
Scattered Judeans return and gather a large harvest.
Johanan warns that Ishmael plans to kill Gedaliah, but Gedaliah disbelieves him.

41.line: Ishmael murders Gedaliah and others, then Johanan rescues the captives, who prepare to flee to Egypt.
more: Ishmael also kills pilgrims and throws bodies into a cistern.
He takes the remaining people captive toward Ammon.
Johanan's forces free them, though Ishmael escapes.
Fearing Babylon, the survivors stop near Bethlehem on the way to Egypt.

42.line: The remnant asks Jeremiah for God's guidance, and God says to stay in Judah rather than flee to Egypt.
more: They vow to obey whatever God says.
After ten days, God promises protection if they remain.
Going to Egypt will bring sword, famine, and pestilence.
Jeremiah warns that they have already chosen to disobey.

43.line: Johanan and the leaders reject Jeremiah's word and take the remnant, including Jeremiah and Baruch, to Egypt.
more: They accuse Baruch of turning Jeremiah against them.
They settle at Tahpanhes.
Jeremiah buries stones at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace.
He announces that Nebuchadnezzar will conquer Egypt and set his throne there.

44.line: Jeremiah rebukes Judeans in Egypt for idolatry, and they defiantly vow to keep worshiping the queen of heaven.
more: God reminds them that Jerusalem fell for such idolatry.
The people claim life was better when they worshiped her.
God swears that only a few will escape back to Judah.
Pharaoh Hophra's defeat is given as the sign.

45.line: God tells Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, not to seek great things for himself but promises to spare his life.
more: Baruch complains of sorrow and weariness.
God is breaking down what he has built.
Baruch will escape with his life wherever he goes.

46.line: Jeremiah foretells Egypt's defeat by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish and Babylon's invasion of Egypt.
more: Egypt's army rises like the Nile but stumbles by the Euphrates.
Egypt will be shamed and handed to a people from the north.
Afterward Egypt will be inhabited as before.
Jacob is told not to fear, for God will save him.

47.line: Jeremiah announces destruction on the Philistines, coming like flood waters from the north.
more: The sword of the LORD will not rest.
Gaza and Ashkelon will be devastated.
Tyre and Sidon will lose their remaining helpers.

48.line: Jeremiah announces judgment on Moab for its pride and its trust in its works and its god Chemosh.
more: Moab's cities will be ruined and its people exiled.
Moab had settled undisturbed, like wine on its dregs.
It magnified itself against the LORD and mocked Israel.
God will restore Moab's fortunes in the latter days.

49.line: Jeremiah pronounces judgment on Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Hazor, and Elam.
more: Ammon will be dispossessed but later restored.
Edom will become a desolation like Sodom and Gomorrah.
Damascus will panic, and Kedar and Hazor will be plundered.
Elam will be scattered, yet restored in the latter days.

50.line: Jeremiah foretells Babylon's fall to a northern nation and the return of Israel and Judah to seek the LORD.
more: Babylon's gods Bel and Merodach will be shamed.
Israel's scattered sheep will be pardoned and restored.
Babylon will be repaid for what it has done.
Israel's Redeemer is strong and will plead their cause.

51.line: Babylon's destruction is announced, and Seraiah sinks Jeremiah's written prophecy in the Euphrates as a sign.
more: God stirs up the kings of the Medes against Babylon.
His people are told to flee from Babylon.
God, the maker of all things, is contrasted with false idols.
The sunken scroll shows Babylon will sink and not rise.

52.line: Jerusalem falls, the temple is plundered and burned, and later Jehoiachin is released from prison in Babylon.
more: Zedekiah's rebellion leads to siege and famine.
He is captured, blinded, and taken to Babylon.
Leaders are executed, and the numbers of exiles are recorded.
Evil-merodach frees Jehoiachin and gives him a place at his table.

Lamentations.line: Lamentations mourns Jerusalem's destruction by Babylon as God's judgment for sin, while holding to hope in God's steadfast love.
more: Five poems grieve the fallen city, most arranged as Hebrew alphabetic acrostics.
Jerusalem is pictured as a desolate widow whose sin brought her ruin.
The poems describe the LORD acting like an enemy against Zion.
The central poem turns to hope in God's mercies, new every morning.
The book ends with a communal prayer for restoration.

1.line: Jerusalem, pictured as a lonely widow, weeps over her ruin and confesses that her sin brought God's judgment.
more: Her lovers and friends have betrayed her, and none comfort her.
Her people are exiled, and her sanctuary has been invaded.
Zion asks passers-by to look and see her sorrow.
She admits the LORD is right and asks him to punish her enemies.

2.line: The LORD in anger has destroyed Zion's walls, temple, king, and priests, and the poet weeps over the suffering.
more: God acted like an enemy, carrying out his long-decreed word.
Children faint from hunger in the streets.
False prophets failed to expose Judah's sin.
Zion is urged to cry out to God for her children.

3.line: A suffering man describes God's affliction, then finds hope in God's steadfast love and calls for repentance.
more: He feels walled in, broken, and unheard.
God's mercies never come to an end and are new every morning.
It is good to wait quietly for the LORD's salvation.
He recalls God's help and asks for justice against his enemies.

4.line: The poet contrasts Zion's former glory with the horrors of siege and fall, ending with Edom's coming judgment.
more: Gold has grown dim, and precious children are treated like clay pots.
Famine drives mothers to cook their own children.
The sins of prophets and priests are blamed.
The king was captured, but Zion's punishment will come to an end.

5.line: The community prays for God to remember their disgrace, confesses sin, and pleads for restoration.
more: They describe foreign rule, hunger, and the abuse of women, princes, and elders.
Joy has ceased, and Mount Zion lies desolate.
They affirm that the LORD reigns forever.
They ask God to restore them and renew their days.

Ezekiel.line: Ezekiel, a priest in exile, announces Jerusalem's fall for its sin, judges the nations, and envisions Israel's restoration and a new temple.
more: Ezekiel sees God's glory in Babylon and is called as a watchman to rebellious Israel.
Through sign-acts and visions, he announces Jerusalem's destruction and God's glory leaving the temple.
He traces Israel's long unfaithfulness and calls each person to repent.
Oracles against surrounding nations, including Tyre and Egypt, show God's rule over all.
After Jerusalem falls, he promises a new heart, a Davidic shepherd, and revived dry bones.
Final visions describe a new temple, God's glory returning, and the land renewed.

1.line: In exile by the Chebar canal, Ezekiel sees four living creatures, wheels, and God's glory above a throne.
more: The vision comes in the fifth year of Jehoiachin's exile.
Each creature has four faces and wings and moves with wheels full of eyes.
Above them sits a figure like a man, radiant like fire.
Ezekiel falls on his face before the glory of the LORD.

2.line: God sends Ezekiel to rebellious Israel and gives him a scroll written with lamentation and woe.
more: The Spirit sets him on his feet to hear God speak.
He must speak whether the people hear or refuse.
He is told not to fear them or be rebellious himself.

3.line: Ezekiel eats the scroll, is appointed a watchman over Israel, and is made mute except when God speaks.
more: The scroll tastes as sweet as honey.
God makes his forehead hard against Israel's stubbornness.
A watchman who fails to warn is held responsible for the blood.
He sits overwhelmed among the exiles at Tel-abib for seven days.

4.line: Ezekiel acts out Jerusalem's siege with a model city and by lying on his sides to bear the people's punishment.
more: He draws Jerusalem on a brick and sets siege works around it.
He lies on his left side 390 days and on his right side 40 days.
He eats rationed bread and water, picturing famine.
God allows him to bake with cow dung instead of human dung.

5.line: Ezekiel shaves his head and divides the hair to show Jerusalem's people dying by fire, sword, and scattering.
more: A third is burned, a third struck with the sword, and a third scattered.
A few hairs are tucked in his robe, yet some of these are burned.
Jerusalem has been more wicked than the nations around her.
God will judge without pity and make the city a reproach.

6.line: Ezekiel prophesies against Israel's mountains, announcing the destruction of idolatrous high places and a surviving remnant.
more: Altars will be broken and the slain laid before their idols.
Some will escape and be scattered among the nations.
The survivors will remember God and loathe themselves for their evils.
Then they will know that he is the LORD.

7.line: Ezekiel announces that the end has come upon the land, with judgment for Israel's abominations.
more: Disaster comes without pity or sparing.
Buying and selling become meaningless, and silver and gold cannot save.
Wealth used for idols will be given to foreigners.
Prophet, priest, and elders will fail to give counsel.

8.line: In a vision Ezekiel is carried to Jerusalem and shown abominations practiced at the temple.
more: He sees an image of jealousy at the north gate.
Seventy elders burn incense to images of creatures in secret.
Women sit weeping for Tammuz at the gate.
About twenty-five men worship the sun with their backs to the temple.

9.line: Executioners strike Jerusalem's idolaters, while a man in linen marks those who grieve over its abominations.
more: Those marked on the forehead are spared.
Judgment begins at the sanctuary with the elders.
Ezekiel pleads, but God says the guilt is exceedingly great.

10.line: God's glory moves to the temple threshold, and the man in linen takes burning coals to scatter over Jerusalem.
more: The coals are taken from between the cherubim.
Ezekiel recognizes the cherubim as the creatures from his Chebar vision.
The glory moves to the east gate with the cherubim and wheels.

11.line: Ezekiel condemns Jerusalem's wicked leaders, hears a promise of a new heart, and sees God's glory leave the city.
more: Pelatiah dies while Ezekiel is prophesying.
God will be a sanctuary for the exiles for a while.
He will give them one heart and a new spirit.
The glory rests on the mountain east of the city, and Ezekiel reports to the exiles.

12.line: Ezekiel acts out going into exile, picturing the prince's flight and capture, and eats with trembling.
more: He packs an exile's baggage and digs through the wall at evening.
The prince will be brought to Babylon yet not see it.
God rejects the proverb that every vision comes to nothing.
His word will be fulfilled without delay.

13.line: Ezekiel condemns false prophets who cry peace and women who practice divination, deceiving God's people.
more: They whitewash a flimsy wall that God will tear down.
They speak lying visions that God did not send.
The women's magic bands and veils ensnare lives.
God will deliver his people from their hands.

14.line: God rejects elders with idols in their hearts and declares that even Noah, Daniel, and Job could save only themselves.
more: Idolaters who inquire of a prophet will be cut off.
A prophet who is deceived will share the punishment.
Four severe judgments are sent on a sinful land.
A surviving remnant will show the justice of God's actions.

15.line: Jerusalem is compared to useless vine wood that will be given to the fire.
more: Vine wood is useless even before it is burned.
The inhabitants escape one fire only to be consumed by another.
The land will be desolate because of their unfaithfulness.

16.line: God portrays Jerusalem as an abandoned infant he raised and married, who became an unfaithful wife, yet promises an everlasting covenant.
more: He adorned her, but she trusted in her beauty and played the whore.
She sacrificed her children and pursued foreign nations.
She is worse than her sisters Samaria and Sodom.
God will remember his covenant and atone for all she has done.

17.line: A riddle of two eagles and a vine depicts Zedekiah's broken treaty with Babylon, followed by a promised cedar sprig.
more: The vine turns toward a second eagle, representing Egypt.
Zedekiah broke his oath and will die in Babylon.
God will plant a tender sprig on a high mountain of Israel.
It will become a noble cedar sheltering every kind of bird.

18.line: God rejects the sour grapes proverb, declaring each person accountable for his own sin and calling Israel to repent.
more: A righteous son will not die for his wicked father's sin.
A wicked man who turns from his sins will live.
God takes no pleasure in anyone's death.
Israel is urged to make for itself a new heart and spirit.

19.line: Ezekiel laments Israel's princes as captured lion cubs and as a vine uprooted and burned.
more: One cub is taken to Egypt and another to Babylon.
The once fruitful vine is replanted in the wilderness.
No strong stem remains to be a ruler's scepter.

20.line: God recounts Israel's rebellion since Egypt, refuses the elders' inquiry, and promises to purge and restore his people.
more: Israel repeatedly profaned God's Sabbaths and worshiped idols.
God held back destruction for the sake of his name.
He will bring them into a wilderness of judgment and purge the rebels.
On his holy mountain he will accept them.

21.line: God draws his sword against Jerusalem, and Babylon's king chooses by divination to attack Jerusalem before Ammon.
more: Ezekiel groans publicly as a sign of coming grief.
The sword is sharpened and polished for slaughter.
The wicked prince's crown will be removed until the rightful one comes.
Ammon will also fall to the sword.

22.line: Jerusalem is charged with bloodshed, idolatry, and injustice, and God will melt it in his furnace.
more: Leaders oppress, and the people profane Sabbaths and holy things.
Israel has become dross to be smelted.
Prophets, priests, princes, and people are all corrupt.
God found no one to stand in the breach.

23.line: Samaria and Jerusalem are portrayed as two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, punished for unfaithful alliances and idolatry.
more: Oholah pursued Assyria and was handed over to it.
Oholibah was worse, lusting after Assyria, Babylon, and Egypt.
Her former lovers will come against her.
She will drink the same cup of ruin as her sister.

24.line: A boiling pot pictures Jerusalem's siege, and Ezekiel is told not to mourn his wife's death as a sign.
more: The siege begins on the very day this word is given.
The corroded pot is heated until its filth is consumed.
The exiles likewise will not mourn the fall of the temple.
A survivor will bring the news, and Ezekiel's mouth will be opened.

25.line: Ezekiel prophesies against Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia for gloating over and taking revenge on Judah.
more: Ammon rejoiced when the sanctuary was profaned.
Moab said Judah is like all the other nations.
Edom and Philistia acted with vengeance.
Each will know the LORD through his judgment.

26.line: God announces that Nebuchadnezzar and many nations will destroy Tyre for rejoicing over Jerusalem's fall.
more: Tyre will become a bare rock for spreading nets.
Its walls and towers will be broken down.
The princes of the coastlands will lament its fall.
Tyre will go down to the pit and never be rebuilt.

27.line: Ezekiel laments Tyre as a magnificent merchant ship that sinks in the heart of the seas.
more: The ship is built from the finest materials.
Many nations traded their goods with Tyre.
An east wind wrecks it with all its cargo.
Sailors and kings mourn its terrible end.

28.line: Ezekiel condemns the proud king of Tyre, laments his fall from Eden, judges Sidon, and promises Israel's regathering.
more: The prince of Tyre claimed to be a god.
In the lament he is pictured as a guardian cherub cast from God's mountain.
Sidon will suffer pestilence and sword.
Israel will dwell securely in its land.

29.line: Ezekiel prophesies against Pharaoh, the great dragon of the Nile, announcing Egypt's desolation and lowly restoration.
more: Egypt was a staff of reed that failed Israel.
Egypt will be desolate forty years, then become a lowly kingdom.
God gives Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as wages for the siege of Tyre.
A horn will spring up for the house of Israel.

30.line: Ezekiel announces the day of the LORD against Egypt and its allies and the breaking of Pharaoh's arms.
more: Egypt's cities and idols will be destroyed.
Nebuchadnezzar is God's instrument of judgment.
God strengthens the arms of Babylon's king but breaks Pharaoh's.
Egyptians will be scattered among the nations.

31.line: Pharaoh is compared to Assyria, a towering cedar cut down for its pride and sent down to Sheol.
more: The cedar surpassed all the trees in Eden.
Its great height made its heart proud.
Foreigners cut it down, and the nations mourned.
Pharaoh and his multitude will share its fate.

32.line: Ezekiel laments Pharaoh as a sea monster caught in a net and describes Egypt joining the slain in the pit.
more: Darkness will cover the heavens over Egypt.
The sword of Babylon's king will come upon it.
Assyria, Elam, Meshech, Tubal, Edom, and Sidon already lie in the pit.
Pharaoh will be comforted only by seeing them.

33.line: Ezekiel is reaffirmed as watchman, hears of Jerusalem's fall, and condemns those who hear his words without obeying.
more: God desires the wicked to turn from his way and live.
Past righteousness or wickedness does not decide a person's end.
A fugitive reports the city's fall, and Ezekiel's mouth is opened.
The people treat him like a singer of love songs.

34.line: God condemns Israel's selfish shepherds and promises to shepherd his flock himself through his servant David.
more: The shepherds fed themselves and let the sheep scatter.
God will seek the lost and judge between sheep and sheep.
One shepherd, his servant David, will tend them.
A covenant of peace will bring security and showers of blessing.

35.line: Ezekiel prophesies against Mount Seir, Edom, for its perpetual enmity and its desire to possess Israel's land.
more: Edom gave Israel over to the sword in its calamity.
Edom boasted against the LORD.
Mount Seir will become a perpetual desolation.

36.line: God promises to restore Israel's mountains and people, cleansing them and giving a new heart and spirit for his name's sake.
more: Nations that mocked Israel will bear their own reproach.
Israel profaned God's name among the nations.
God will sprinkle clean water on them and put his Spirit within them.
The desolate land will become like the garden of Eden.

37.line: Ezekiel sees dry bones come to life and joins two sticks, picturing Israel's revival and reunion under David.
more: He prophesies, and breath enters the bones.
The bones represent the whole house of Israel.
The sticks for Judah and Joseph become one in his hand.
God promises an everlasting covenant and his sanctuary among them.

38.line: God announces that Gog of the land of Magog will invade restored Israel in the latter days and be destroyed.
more: Gog leads many nations against a land living in security.
God brings Gog to display his holiness before the nations.
A great earthquake shakes the land.
Pestilence, bloodshed, hail, and fire destroy Gog's army.

39.line: Gog's army falls on Israel's mountains, its weapons are burned, and God promises to restore Israel and pour out his Spirit.
more: Israel burns the weapons as fuel for seven years.
Burying the dead takes seven months in the Valley of Hamon-gog.
Birds and beasts are summoned to a sacrificial feast.
The nations will know Israel went into exile for its sin.

40.line: In a vision Ezekiel is taken to Israel, where a bronze-like man measures a new temple's gates and courts.
more: The vision comes in the twenty-fifth year of the exile.
Ezekiel is told to declare everything he sees to Israel.
Gates, chambers, and tables for sacrifices are described.
Rooms are set apart for the priests, the sons of Zadok.

41.line: The measuring continues with the temple's nave, Most Holy Place, side chambers, and carved decorations.
more: The Most Holy Place measures twenty cubits square.
Side chambers surround the temple in three stories.
Walls and doors are carved with cherubim and palm trees.
A wooden altar is called the table that is before the LORD.

42.line: Ezekiel is shown holy chambers for the priests and the outer wall separating the holy from the common.
more: Priests eat the most holy offerings in these chambers.
They change garments there before going out to the people.
The surrounding wall forms a square, five hundred cubits on each side.

43.line: God's glory returns through the east gate and fills the temple, and the altar's design and consecration are given.
more: Ezekiel compares this vision to his earlier ones and falls on his face.
God will dwell among Israel forever, and they must put away defilement.
The whole mountaintop around the temple is to be most holy.
Seven days of offerings consecrate the altar.

44.line: The east gate stays shut because the LORD entered by it, and duties are assigned to Levites and Zadokite priests.
more: Only the prince may sit in the gate to eat bread before the LORD.
Foreigners uncircumcised in heart are excluded from the sanctuary.
Levites who went astray serve as keepers, while the sons of Zadok minister at the altar.
Rules cover the priests' clothing, marriage, purity, and portions.

45.line: A holy district of land is set apart for the sanctuary, priests, Levites, city, and prince, with laws for offerings and feasts.
more: Princes must stop oppression and use just weights and measures.
The people give offerings to the prince.
The prince provides offerings for feasts, new moons, and Sabbaths.
Passover and the feast in the seventh month are prescribed.

46.line: Regulations govern the prince's worship, the people's entry and exit, the prince's land, and the temple kitchens.
more: The inner east gate opens on Sabbaths and new moons.
Worshipers leave by the gate opposite the one they entered.
Gifts of land to servants return to the prince in the year of liberty.
Priests boil and bake offerings in designated kitchens.

47.line: A river flows from the temple, growing deeper and making salt waters fresh, and the land's boundaries are set.
more: The water rises from ankle-deep to a river too deep to cross.
Fish abound, though the marshes are left for salt.
Trees on its banks bear fruit monthly and leaves for healing.
Sojourners among Israel receive an inheritance with the tribes.

48.line: The land is divided among the twelve tribes around a holy portion, and the city is named The LORD Is There.
more: Seven tribes lie north and five south of the holy portion.
The holy portion includes the sanctuary and lands for priests, Levites, and the city.
The prince's land lies on both sides of the holy portion.
The city has twelve gates named for the tribes of Israel.
